title: REQUESTS
description:
REQUESTS is the Python HTTP client module and dependency referenced throughout the documentation examples and tests. It is imported explicitly with `import requests`, accessed through statements such as `from requests import hooks` and `from requests import Request, Session`, and frequently referenced as the `requests` module namespace. Some excerpts show only qualified references without the corresponding import statement, while several references occur in documentation examples rather than visible production code.

The module provides APIs for constructing and sending HTTP requests, including `requests.get`, `requests.post`, `requests.put`, `requests.patch`, `requests.delete`, `requests.head`, `requests.options`, and the general `requests.request` function. It supports request construction through `requests.Request`, persistent client behavior through `requests.Session`, adapter configuration through `requests.adapters.HTTPAdapter`, streaming responses, proxy configuration, OAuth-related requests, and access to HTTP status codes such as `requests.codes.ok`.

REQUESTS also supplies response and exception-related interfaces, including `requests.Response`, `requests.exceptions.ConnectionError`, `requests.exceptions.JSONDecodeError`, and `requests.exceptions.SSLError`, as well as the `requests.sessions.get_netrc_auth` helper. Overall, REQUESTS is used as the HTTP client namespace for request execution, session management, response handling, status-code inspection, authentication and proxy behavior, adapter configuration, and error handling.

title: REQUESTS.GET
description:
`REQUESTS.GET` is an externally defined callable exposed through the `requests` module for issuing HTTP GET requests and returning response objects. Its implementation and runtime receiver binding are not visible in the provided material.

The callable is used in documentation, examples, and tests for direct HTTP and HTTPS requests, including URLs such as `https://api.github.com/events`, GitHub issue and comments endpoints, `https://example.org`, `https://www.python.org`, `https://httpbin.org/get`, and locally constructed or test-server URLs. Calls may include query parameters, headers, cookies, proxies, timeouts, and authentication credentials.

`REQUESTS.GET` supports examples involving basic authentication, digest authentication, generic authentication objects, optional authentication, redirects, secure redirects, TLS certificate verification, client certificates, and proxy configuration. It is also used with streaming responses, hooks, gzip content, Unicode content, malformed chunked responses, conflicting headers, byte streams, and HTTP status endpoints such as 404 responses.

Typical calls include `requests.get(url)`, `requests.get(url, params=payload)`, `requests.get(url, auth=auth)`, `requests.get(..., auth=('user', 'pass'))`, `requests.get(..., headers=...)`, `requests.get(..., timeout=5)`, `requests.get(..., timeout=None)`, `requests.get(..., verify=...)`, `requests.get(..., cert=...)`, `requests.get(..., proxies=proxies)`, `requests.get(..., hooks=...)`, and `requests.get(..., stream=True)`. The returned response is commonly assigned to a local variable such as `r`, after which examples inspect status codes, parse response content, or evaluate cookies and other response properties.

The callable is explicitly invoked in tests covering invalid URLs, redirects, streaming behavior, authentication, TLS verification, request headers, hooks, entry-point availability, and other HTTP behaviors. Although the examples describe expected timeout and response behavior, they do not provide evidence of production execution or reveal the underlying implementation.

title: R.JSON
description: R.JSON refers to the response method `r.json()`, which is used to decode an HTTP response body into parsed JSON data, including comments responses and authenticated comment responses. The method is also exercised in tests for valid JSON and for responses with absent content, such as HTTP 204 responses. When the response contains valid JSON, `r.json()` returns the decoded data, typically as a JSON object. When the content is invalid or absent, it raises `requests.exceptions.JSONDecodeError`. The available descriptions explicitly reference the callable but do not establish the concrete runtime class of the response receiver `r`, its owning class, or the method’s definition.

title: R.HEADERS
description: R.HEADERS refers to the response attribute `r.headers`, which is used as a mapping-like interface for accessing HTTP response headers. The examples retrieve the `content-type` header with `r.headers['content-type']`, use the capitalization variant `r.headers['Content-Type']`, retrieve it safely with `r.headers.get('content-type')`, and access the `link` header. In one example, `r.headers` is read from a response returned by `requests.head(url=url)`. The concrete runtime class or receiver type of `r` is not established by the available descriptions.

title: R.ENCODING
description: R.ENCODING is an attribute referenced through `r.encoding` and assigned with values such as `'ISO-8859-1'` or documented as `'utf-8'`. It controls the character encoding used when accessing `r.text`. However, the attribute’s receiver binding and runtime type are not defined or visible in the available context, so its implementation and default behavior cannot be confirmed.

title: R.TEXT
description: R.TEXT refers to the `text` attribute of a local response object named `r`. It exposes the response body as decoded text, typically represented as a string containing JSON-like content. Documentation examples reference `r.text` after authentication, cookie, and POST requests, including responses such as `{"authenticated": true, ...}` and `{"cookies": {"cookies_are": "working"}}`. The POST example explicitly prints it with `print(r.text)`. The concrete runtime type and class implementation providing `R.TEXT` are not visible.

title: URLLIB3
description: URLLIB3 is an external Python dependency used by the surrounding HTTP functionality. It provides connection pooling, keep-alive behavior, HTTP response handling, and adapter integration through classes such as `Retry` and `ProxyManager`. Its `urllib3.util.Retry` utility is documented as supporting retry configuration, including situations where multiple addresses may be attempted sequentially. The module is explicitly imported in several contexts, with its `__version__` attribute read for compatibility checks, and the module name supplied to `__import__` while traversing `sys.modules` during compatibility processing. It is also referenced through its namespace for exception classes used in parameterized response-stream tests. Some documentation and test references mention `urllib3` without showing a corresponding import or implementation in the available code, and the module definition itself is not visible in the provided material.

title: SESSION
description: `SESSION` refers to the `requests.Session` class, defined as `Session(SessionRedirectMixin)` and instantiated as `Session()` or `requests.Session()`. It provides persistent session-level behavior across HTTP requests, including cookie and parameter persistence, connection pooling, and request configuration. Session state, such as cookies, is applied when requests are prepared, allowing subsequent requests to reuse shared settings and connection resources.

description: The method spelling `Session.get` is explicitly referenced through calls such as `s.get('https://httpbin.org/cookies')`; the receiver is the local example variable `s`, initialized from `Session`, and the method definition is not visible here.

title: REQUEST
description: `REQUEST` refers to the `Request` class used to represent and configure HTTP requests. In some contexts, `Request` is explicitly imported from the `requests` package and instantiated for `POST` requests with `Request('POST', url, data=data, headers=headers)` or for `GET` requests with `Request('GET', url, data=data, headers=headers)`, although the imported class’s definition is not visible there. In the provided implementation, the exact `Request` class inherits from `RequestHooksMixin`; its constructor stores the request configuration, `__repr__` formats the HTTP method for representation, and `prepare` constructs and prepares a corresponding `PreparedRequest`.

title: REQUEST.PREPARE
description: `REQUEST.PREPARE` refers to the `Request.prepare` method. The method constructs a `PreparedRequest` object, passes the request configuration and hooks to its `prepare(...)` method, and returns the prepared request. It is invoked through expressions such as `req.prepare()` and `r.prepare()`, although some references do not establish the receiver’s concrete class or runtime binding. In usage, the returned prepared request is assigned to `prepped`, after which its body and headers may be modified before it is sent.

title: RESPONSE
description: `Response` is a class that models the HTTP response returned by a server for an HTTP request. It contains information about the server’s response and the original `Request`, including response attributes and related metadata. The class defines initialization behavior, context-manager support, serialization hooks, truthiness evaluation, iteration, and properties associated with redirects. It is referenced as `Response <requests.Response>` and represents the response object exposed by the requests framework.

title: PREPAREDREQUEST
description: `PreparedRequest` is the prepared HTTP request object produced before transmission and used internally by API or session calls. Response objects expose the corresponding prepared request through their `request` attribute. The `PreparedRequest` class inherits from `RequestEncodingMixin` and `RequestHooksMixin`, and its constructor initializes the request method, URL, headers, cookies, and body state to `None` before those values are populated.

title: PRINT
description: PRINT is an explicitly referenced built-in or external callable whose definition is not visible in the provided material. It is used throughout code and documentation examples to display values, including HTTP response information such as `WWW-Authenticate` headers, response URLs, response bodies (`r.content`, `r.text`, and `r1.text`), response headers, decoded JSON values, parsed commit-data values, streamed lines, JSON strings, and `DEFAULT_CA_BUNDLE_PATH`. PRINT is also called to output the result of `where()` when the module runs under the `__name__ == "__main__"` condition, and it is invoked by `main()` and `print_url()` for output. The examples demonstrate its use for presentation and debugging, but do not reveal its implementation.

title: REQUESTS.SESSION
description:
`REQUESTS.SESSION` refers to the externally defined Requests library session APIs, primarily the `requests.Session` class/constructor and the `requests.session()` callable. Their implementations are not visible in the available source or documentation context.

The `requests.Session()` constructor is used throughout the tests and examples to create persistent HTTP session objects. These sessions are configured with default headers, cookies, proxies, redirect limits, response hooks, TLS-related settings, and mounted HTTP adapters. They are also used for sending authenticated and general requests, rebuilding proxies, testing redirect behavior, pickling, adapter lookup, connection cleanup, and other session-level behavior. In some tests, a constructed session is assigned to a variable such as `s` and then used through the local session object.

`requests.Session` is also referenced as the superclass of `CustomRedirectSession`, indicating that custom session implementations can extend the Requests session class. Documentation examples show `requests.Session()` being used to configure default headers, although those examples do not establish production execution.

The related `requests.session()` callable is explicitly invoked in multiple authentication and redirect tests, including `test_HTTP_302_TOO_MANY_REDIRECTS_WITH_PARAMS`, `test_unconsumed_session_response_closes_connection`, and `TestRequests.test_entry_points`, to create session objects. Although the class constructor and lowercase callable are distinct spellings, both represent externally provided Requests mechanisms for creating HTTP sessions.

title: REQUESTS.POST
description:
`REQUESTS.POST` refers to the externally defined public callable `requests.post`, whose implementation is not visible in the provided material. It is used as the primary entry point for sending HTTP POST requests, including standard form submissions, JSON requests, multipart file uploads, encoded payloads, generator-based uploads, chunked requests, redirect scenarios, and streaming operations.

The callable accepts a target URL and supports request options such as `data`, `json`, `files`, `params`, `auth`, headers, and streaming-related arguments. The `data` argument can contain dictionaries or lists of tuples, which are automatically form-encoded, JSON-encoded content, file-like objects, or generators for upload and chunked-transfer use cases. The `json` argument is used to submit structured JSON payloads, while `files` enables multipart uploads, including multiple files. Some examples also provide query parameters, custom `Host` headers, or optional streaming behavior.

Examples invoke it with URLs such as `https://httpbin.org/post` or helper-generated HTTPBin endpoints, including calls like `requests.post(url, data=body)`, `requests.post(url, json=payload)`, and `requests.post(url, files=files)`. The returned response may be assigned to a local variable for inspection. In authentication tests, posting a comment without authentication produces status `404`, while supplying `HTTPBasicAuth` produces status `201`. Other tests exercise POST requests involving form data, files, redirects, upload generators, and entry-point availability.

title: REQUESTS.RESPONSE
description:

It is documented as the return type for request functions, HTTP verb methods, `send`, and `build_response`, and appears in qualified documentation references for response attributes and methods such as `Response.raise_for_status` and `Response.iter_lines`. The class is also used in examples showing representations such as `<Response [200]>`.

Within the referenced code and tests, `requests.Response` is used in `isinstance` assertions and is explicitly instantiated, including when constructing responses for HTTP error assertions. Some documentation refers to the response class through `Response <requests.Response>`, while one implementation separately instantiates an unresolved `Response` symbol in the visible chunk. The actual definition and implementation of `requests.Response` are external and are not included in the available code.

The method iterates over and yields chunks of a response body. Its usage includes configurable chunk sizes, including integer values, `None`, and the string `"1024"`, as well as the `decode_unicode=True` option for decoding yielded content. title: OPEN
description:
OPEN refers to several file-opening callables referenced throughout the code and documentation. These include the built-in `open` function, used to open the current file with `open(__file__, "rb")`, read `requirements-dev.txt` for multipart file-upload tests, obtain binary upload bodies such as `open("massive-body", "rb")`, and create binary output files with `open(filename, "wb")`. Multipart examples also use it to open files such as `report.xls` and `foo.png`; uploaded files are recommended to be opened in binary mode.

The exact definitions of these built-in or external `open` references are not visible in the available context. In addition, `codecs.open` is referenced for reading files with an explicitly specified encoding, while `file_obj.open(mode)` refers to an object method that opens or configures a file-like object.

title: INT
description:
INT refers to Python’s built-in `int` type and callable. It is used for type checks, conversions, validation, and numeric comparisons across several contexts. `INT` appears in `isinstance(value, (str, bytes, bool, int))` to recognize integer values, and in `isinstance(cookie.expires, int)` to determine whether a cookie expiration is already represented as an integer. It is also used to validate the `chunk_size` argument supplied to `iter_content`.

As a conversion callable, `INT` converts version components before numeric comparisons, normalizes the Windows registry `ProxyEnable` value with `int(winreg.QueryValueEx(...)[0])`, converts redirect values through `int(self.redirects.pop(0))`, and parses the HTTP `content-length` header with `int(r.headers['content-length'])` before comparing it against `TOO_LONG`. Additionally, it converts a cookie’s `max-age` value and uses the resulting number of seconds in a calculation based on `time.time()`.

The definition of `INT` is not visible because it refers to the built-in Python `int` rather than a locally defined entity.

Accessing it triggers a deferred download when the body has not yet been consumed and blocks until the entire response has been downloaded. `Response.__getstate__` accesses `self.content` to ensure that the response content has been fully consumed before state handling. It is also handled when converting registry values in `proxy_bypass_registry`, converting CIDR masks in `is_valid_cidr`, parsing a cookie’s `"max-age"` value, processing JSON serialization through `complexjson.dumps`, and checking cryptography compatibility through `_check_cryptography`. The exception is raised for unsupported hook events and caught by `deregister_hook` during hook removal. It serves as an inherited base class for the externally defined exceptions `MissingSchema`, `InvalidSchema`, `InvalidURL`, and `InvalidHeader`. The provided material references `ValueError` extensively but does not include its definition, indicating that it is supplied by the surrounding Python runtime or an external module.

Across these contexts, `LIST` consistently represents the standard built-in mechanism for creating concrete list objects or checking list-typed results. Its implementation is not visible in the provided code fragments because it is a Python built-in rather than a locally defined symbol.

ISINSTANCE also validates framework- and library-specific objects. These include `CookieJar`, `RequestsCookieJar`, `Morsel`, `MyCookiePolicy`, `Mapping`, `Callable`, `requests.Response`, `builtin_str`, `basestring`, `compat.bytes`, `compat.str`, `integer_types`, timeout exceptions, `MaxRetryError.reason`, and other exception types. It supports logic for cookie updates and merging, case-insensitive dictionary comparisons, request preparation, URL encoding, multipart file encoding, body rewinding, response handling, retry behavior, and status-error processing.

In addition, ISINSTANCE appears in assertions that verify cookie jars, request and response histories, cookie expiration values, response objects, prepared-request body positions, and JSON-decoding compatibility. It is also used to inspect response content and validate `chunk_size` and related content-processing conditions. The callable is referenced as the standard built-in `isinstance`; its implementation is not defined or visible in the provided material.

`PYTEST.MARK.PARAMETRIZE` is the externally defined pytest decorator referenced throughout the visible test suite as `@pytest.mark.parametrize`.
